t: Playing Amal: A Boy at the Window
and Me
Dakghar
(in English,
The Post Office

), a play by Rabindranath Tagore, is about Amal, a young boy who is ill and not allowed to leave his adoptive uncle Madhav’s house. He sits in the courtyard and talks to everyone who passes by, asking where they are going and what they have seen. He wishes

that when he recovers, he will go outside and visit the mountains, and watch the village women carrying water pots back from the mountain waterfalls. He wants to embrace every profession he comes across, sometimes the night watchman, sometimes the hawker.

When a new post office opens nearby, he starts dreaming that the King will send him a letter, or that he might become the King’s postman. The village headman teases him and pretends the King’s letter has come. In the end the royal physician does arrive, b

ut Amal falls asleep for eternity. It is a quiet play, but it says a lot about how a child can be shut inside four walls and still carry the whole world in his imagination. It symbolizes not only children but all of us. We have countless imaginations and d
reams, but we are tied to many things that confine us in small spaces, and still the hope is there to keep wishing and moving toward something.
Tagore wrote the play in 1912 in just four days, according to a
catalogue of Indian theatre at the University of Wisconsin
. The name is simple:
dak
means mail or post, and
ghar
means house, so it is
literally the house where letters live. You can read more about
Tagore’s work in theatre
by Ananda Lal.
The play has travelled far beyond Bengal. Its world premiere was in English, at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in May 1913, even before it was staged in Bengali. The English version was translated by
Devabrata
Mukherjee, with an introduction
by W. B. Yeats. Its most moving performance came in 1942, in the Warsaw Ghetto.
Janusz Korczak
, the doctor

who ran a Jewish orphanage there, had the children perform it on 18 July 1942. The children in the orphanage identified with Amal and, with bated breath, they awaited, together with Amal, the king’s letter that would spell redemption.
Korczak
wanted his c
hildren to learn how to welcome the Angel of Death calmly, and this was his way of conveying this message, as
Yad Vashem’s teaching materials
explain. People keep returning to the play because of its hope and love of life. If you want to read it in English, th
e translation is free on
Project Gutenberg
. It is short and easy to read, so it is a good place to start.
I feel privileged to have played Ama
l, because I connect with him deeply. Since childhood, I wanted to be many things. Sometimes a pilot flying around the world, sometimes a mountaineer like
Wasfia Nazreen

, and sometimes I only wished to be close to people, to watch what they do, to learn what they value, and to be part of it. I love watching people in their passion, and like Amal, I wish to embrace all.
This play a

lso gave me something very special. When I joined theater school (workshop), I kept it a secret from my father because theater is not always appreciated in our societal-religious context, and I knew I might face difficulties. So, when I got admitted to uni

versity and was allowed to go outside alone, I enrolled in an eight-month theater course, which was near my house. Since my parents were both working, I was in charge of taking care of my younger sister and wasn't allowed to leave her home alone. I started
taking her to my theater classes. The school only admitted students at eighteen; considering my
situation,  she
was accepted at twelve years old.
Perhaps that is why our director,
Rabeya
Rabu, chose
Dakghar
in the end for final stage production, a play wi

th room for every age of us. Acting on the same stage as my sister and my closest friends was one of the most memorable experiences of my life. It was so intense. It wasn’t just a production for me; it embodied a hope I had nurtured since childhood. I have

always been curious about the world, eager to learn and explore new things, much like Amal in the play. I know I am not alone here. We all feel same. Now, I often find myself returning to the story of
Dakghar
; it reminds me that no matter the confines we
may face, we must hope; we keep imagining.
